q: Which residue, invisible to a guest, will flatten the mousse of a sparkling wine within seconds of the pour?
exp: Surfactants break bubble walls as they form, so a technically clean glass can kill a Champagne. It is the commonest reason a good sparkling wine looks lifeless.

q: The label is turned toward one person at the table before the foil is cut. Why that person?
opts: They are seated closest to the sommelier station
They ordered the wine and can confirm it
They are the eldest person among the guests
They are expected to settle the whole bill
exp: Presentation is the last cheap moment to catch a wrong vintage or a wrong producer, and the person who ordered is the only one at the table who knows what was chosen. Once the capsule is cut the bottle belongs to the restaurant.

q: A table of ten empties the first bottle and a second of the same wine is fetched. What has to happen before it reaches anyone's glass?
accept: present and taste the new bottle
the host tastes the new bottle
offer the host a fresh taste
pour a fresh taste for the host
ans: The new bottle is presented and tasted before any is poured
exp: Every bottle carries its own risk, so the second is shown and sampled exactly as the first was. The taste goes into a clean glass, since a glass holding the dregs of bottle one will mask a fault in bottle two. Pouring first and checking afterwards spreads a spoiled wine across the whole table at once.

q: From which side of a seated guest is a glass filled in classical restaurant service?
exp: Beverages go to the right, where the glassware sits, and food to the left. Working the wrong side puts an arm across the guest.

q: A guest tastes and says the wine is not to their liking, though nothing is wrong with it. What is the correct handling?
opts: Explain that the wine is sound and ask them to persevere with it
Replace it without argument and put both bottles on the bill
Ask the rest of the table to decide whether it stays
Take it away, offer an alternative, and absorb the cost
exp: Soundness is the test for a fault, but a disliked bottle is a commercial question rather than a technical one. Most of an opened bottle can be recovered by the glass, which is why the wine costs the house far less than an argument at the table does.

q: A firm young red and a fragile old one are poured across a single meal. Which goes into the glass first?
exp: Order protects the more delicate bottle. A firm young red after an old one flattens it, while the reverse merely flatters the young wine.

q: Glasses are exchanged rather than reused when a table moves from a white to a red. What is that avoiding?
opts: A licensing requirement covering glassware
Residue of the first wine altering the second
A glass too small to hold a full measure
The second wine arriving at the wrong temperature
exp: Even a teaspoon of an aromatic white shows in a Pinot Noir. Where a fresh glass is impossible, a splash of the new wine is used to rinse the old one out.

q: Stations, tools and glassware are set in place before the first guest arrives. Which French term covers that preparation?
exp: The phrase travels from the kitchen to the floor unchanged. A sommelier hunting for a decanter mid-service failed an hour before the doors opened.

q: Which corkscrew, carrying a foil blade and a two-step lever, is the tool actually carried in the pocket?
exp: The second notch on the lever is what makes it work, letting a long cork come out in two controlled stages rather than one wrenching pull.

q: Cutting the capsule below the lower lip rather than above it prevents what?
opts: Wine touching foil on its way into the glass
The cork breaking apart inside the neck
Sediment being stirred back into suspension
The label tearing when the bottle is presented
exp: Old lead capsules made this a health point and modern ones make it a question of taste and tidiness. The cut also looks deliberate rather than hacked.

q: The worm has entered off-centre and the cork is beginning to tear. What is the least damaging recovery?
opts: Drive the worm all the way through the cork and pull hard
Push the remains of the cork into the bottle and pour at once
Ease off, re-angle the worm down the same channel, and lift slowly
Warm the neck of the bottle in a hot cloth to loosen the cork
exp: Speed is what destroys a cork. Going back down the channel already cut keeps the remaining cork whole instead of drilling a second hole through it, and the lift comes straight up rather than at an angle.

q: A fifty-year-old cork crumbles at the first turn of the worm. Which two-pronged extractor exists for exactly this?
exp: The blades slide down either side of the cork and grip it whole, which is the only chance with a cork a worm would simply pulverise.

q: The pour is finishing and a drop is about to run down the shoulder. Which movement of the bottle prevents it?
accept: a twist of the bottle as it is lifted
ans: A twist of the bottle as it is lifted
exp: A small turn as the neck comes up carries the last drop back over the lip. A serviette in the other hand covers whatever the turn misses.

q: Warm from a delivery and opened straight away, a bottle pushes its own cork up the moment the cage comes off. What is the correct move?
accept: keep a hand on the cork and ease it out slowly
keep a hand on the cork
hold the cork and ease it out
hold it down and ease it out slowly
keep hold of the cork and ease it out
ease it out slowly under the thumb
keep pressure on the cork and let it out slowly
hold the cork down and ease it out slowly
keep a hand on it and ease it out slowly
keep your thumb on it and ease it out
keep a thumb on the cork and ease it out
ans: Keep a hand on the cork and ease it out slowly
exp: Pressure climbs steeply as a bottle warms, and a cork already on the move will not be re-seated. Take the weight of it, point the neck at a wall rather than at the room, and walk it out under the thumb until the gas sighs away. The bottle then goes back into ice before anything is poured, because a warm sparkling wine foams out of the glass as well.

q: A thumb stays over the cork from the instant the cage is loosened. What is that guarding against?
opts: A cork leaving under six atmospheres of pressure
The bottle warming in the hand
Wine foaming out over the lip of the bottle
The wire scratching the label
exp: A Champagne bottle sits at roughly six atmospheres, pressure comparable to a heavy vehicle tyre, and the cork gives no warning. Eye injuries from sparkling corks are reported every year.

q: A loud report and a plume of foam mark a badly opened sparkling bottle. Which sound should the opening aim for?
exp: The bang is escaping gas that ought to have stayed dissolved in the wine. A controlled release leaves the mousse where the guest can drink it.
